summary: This informational document describes a routing scenario in which IPv4 packets travel over an IPv6 network, using the methods of RFCs 6145 and 6052. It uses a separate OSPFv3 routing table for IPv4-embedded IPv6 routes.

eli5.summary: Old-style packets travel across a new-style network by dressing up as new-style ones, and routers keep a separate map for that.

subtitle: Transporting IPv4 packets across an IPv6 network using address translation

tldr.problem: Organizations need to interconnect separate IPv4-only networks through an IPv6 backbone, but routing protocols designed for IPv4 do not work directly over IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: Translate IPv4 packets into IPv4-embedded IPv6 packets at border routers, route them through the IPv6 network using OSPFv3, then translate them back to IPv4 at the destination.
tldr.outcome: Allows IPv4 networks to communicate across an IPv6-only core network without tunnels or IBGP, simplifying operations.

today: RFC 6992 is an informational document describing a proven operational technique for IPv4-IPv6 coexistence. It remains applicable for organizations deploying IPv6 backbones while maintaining IPv4 client networks, offering an alternative to tunneling approaches.

sections.title: The Routing Problem
sections.content:
Due to IPv4 address exhaustion, organizations need to transition to IPv6 networks. In the meantime, many have IPv4-only networks that must coexist with new IPv6-only infrastructure. When an organization wants to use an IPv6-only network as a backbone to interconnect multiple separate IPv4 networks, those IPv4 packets must somehow traverse the IPv6 core. This document describes a routing solution using Address Family Translation Border Routers (AFXLBRs) that convert IPv4 packets to IPv6 and back, allowing IPv4 reachability information to flow through the IPv6 network using OSPFv3.

The approach differs from earlier tunnel-based solutions (like RFC 5565) by avoiding the need for IBGP and mesh tunnels. Instead, AFXLBRs use stateless translation and a dedicated OSPFv3 routing instance to route IPv4-embedded IPv6 packets through the IPv6 network, simplifying deployment and operation.
sections.eli5: Instead of using fancy tunnels, we put old-style addresses inside new-style ones and use the normal routing system to move them.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
The core concept is the IPv4-embedded IPv6 address, defined in RFC 6052. An operator chooses an IPv6 prefix (either the well-known prefix 64:ff9b::/96 or a locally allocated prefix of length 32, 40, 48, 56, or 64) and embeds each IPv4 address within it. For example, an IPv4 address might be embedded by prepending the IPv6 prefix to the 32-bit IPv4 address. This allows IPv4 networks to be represented as IPv6 destinations within the backbone.

An AFXLBR is a border router that sits at the edge of an IPv4 network and the IPv6 backbone. It understands both IPv4 and IPv6, and can perform stateless header translation between the two formats using RFC 6145. When an AFXLBR receives an IPv4 packet destined for a remote IPv4 network, it translates the IPv4 header to an IPv6 header, converting the IPv4 addresses into IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses, then forwards the resulting IPv6 packet into the backbone.
sections.eli5: Border routers take old-style addresses, wrap them as special new-style addresses, and change the packet headers to match.

sections.title: Routing with OSPFv3
sections.content:
Rather than flooding IPv4-embedded IPv6 routes throughout the entire IPv6 network, a separate OSPFv3 routing instance is created solely for these routes. This instance uses a private Instance ID in the range 192-255 (reserved for private use per RFC 6969) and operates only on AFXLBRs and a set of provider routers (P routers) that form the IPv4-embedded IPv6 topology. This subtopology is typically smaller than the full IPv6 network, reducing the routing table burden on routers that do not participate in the interconnection.

IPv4-embedded IPv6 routes are advertised as AS-External-LSAs through OSPFv3, allowing the metric and reliability characteristics of IPv4 routes to be preserved in the IPv6 network. The routing solution allows traffic to take advantage of multiple paths across the backbone and benefits from OSPFv3's convergence properties, without requiring tunnels or additional protocols.
sections.eli5: A special routing map is created just for the wrapped addresses, and only the routers that need to know about them learn those routes.

sections.title: Packet Translation and Forwarding
sections.content:
When an AFXLBR receives an IPv4 packet from a connected client network destined for another client network, it performs three actions: it translates the source IPv4 address to an IPv4-embedded IPv6 address, translates the destination IPv4 address to an IPv4-embedded IPv6 address, and translates the IPv4 header to an IPv6 header (adjusting fields like TTL and protocol number). The resulting IPv6 packet is forwarded to the destination AFXLBR by normal IPv6 routing, guided by the dedicated IPv4-embedded IPv6 routing table.

At the destination AFXLBR, the reverse process occurs: the embedded IPv4 addresses are extracted from the IPv6 destination and source addresses, the IPv6 header is translated back to an IPv4 header, and the resulting IPv4 packet is forwarded according to the destination AFXLBR's IPv4 routing table. Because translation is stateless, there is no per-flow state required at either border router, and packets can be processed rapidly.
sections.eli5: At each border, packets change clothes: incoming old-style packets put on new-style wrappings, travel through the network, then change back at the far border.

sections.title: Deployment and Operational Aspects
sections.content:
Before deployment, the operator must decide which routers participate in the IPv4-embedded IPv6 topology. All AFXLBRs must be part of this topology, but only a subset of provider routers need to be included based on desired redundancy and path diversity. The topology must be continuous with no partitions, and each AFXLBR must have at least one connection to a provider router or another AFXLBR. The operator must also configure the IPv6 prefix used for embedding IPv4 addresses consistently across all AFXLBRs.

MTU differences between the IPv6 backbone and IPv4 client networks require attention. Since IPv6 routers do not fragment packets, AFXLBRs should use path MTU discovery to determine safe packet sizes and propagate MTU information back into IPv4 client networks. Route aggregation reduces the number of routes advertised into the IPv6 backbone. Loop prevention mechanisms (using the DN bit from RFC 4576) ensure that LSAs sent from AFXLBRs into client networks are not reflected back into the IPv6 network, preventing routing loops.
sections.eli5: Operators must pick the right routers for the path, choose the wrapping format, and manage size and loop issues.
